summary: A 1978 April 1st RFC that jokes about a Telnet option called RANDOMLY-LOSE, a mock option where one side asks permission to lose data at random. It is humorous, not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke rule where a computer asks politely if it may lose your messages for no reason. Please do not use it.

questions: what is the randomly lose telnet option
why was rfc 748 published on april 1st
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing a Telnet option to lose data randomly

tldr.problem: Several ARPANET hosts appeared to provide undocumented random lossage such as system crashes, lost data, and incorrect program behavior as part of their normal operation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 748 proposes a TELNET option, RANDOMLY-LOSE (code 256), that lets servers ask permission from clients to randomly lose data, or clients request that servers do so. The negotiation follows the standard TELNET option protocol (WILL, WON'T, DO, DON'T commands).
tldr.outcome: This April 1st joke satirizes the unreliability of early computer systems by proposing to make random failure an official negotiated service.

today: RFC 748 is a historically significant April Fools' joke that provides a snapshot of frustrations with early ARPANET reliability. No implementation adopted the option, and it should never be implemented. Modern systems have far better reliability and error handling than the hosts of the 1970s. However, the RFC remains a humorous and poignant reminder of how difficult network systems were to work with when they were new.

sections.title: A Proposal for Managed Unreliability
sections.content:
RFC 748 is an April 1st joke published on 1 April 1978. It proposes a new TELNET option called RANDOMLY-LOSE that lets systems request and grant permission to randomly lose data.

The RFC opens by observing that several ARPANET hosts appeared to provide "random lossage, such as system crashes, lost data, incorrectly functioning programs, etc., as part of their services." These services were often undocumented and confusing to users. The joke is that these failures should be formalized, negotiated, and made official.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April Fools' joke from 1978. It pretends that randomly breaking things should be an official feature of computer networks that you can turn on or off.

sections.title: The RANDOMLY-LOSE Option
sections.content:
The option uses TELNET's standard negotiation protocol. A server sends IAC WILL RANDOMLY-LOSE to request permission to randomly lose data, and the client replies with IAC DO RANDOMLY-LOSE to grant permission or IAC DON'T RANDOMLY-LOSE to forbid it.

Alternatively, a client can request that the server randomly lose by sending IAC DO RANDOMLY-LOSE, and the server replies with IAC WILL RANDOMLY-LOSE (agreeing) or IAC WON'T RANDOMLY-LOSE (insisting on being reliable). The default is WON'T and DON'T, meaning no random loss unless negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke follows real TELNET option rules: one side says "may I randomly lose data?" and the other side says yes or no.

sections.title: The Satire
sections.content:
The real point of the joke is that many ARPANET hosts in 1978 were unreliable: they crashed, lost data, or behaved incorrectly without warning or good reason. Some of these failures were due to bugs; others were due to hardware limitations or operating system quirks. Users had no way to predict or disable these failures.

By proposing that random lossage be made an official, negotiated TELNET option, the RFC humorously suggests that chaos should be formalized and controllable—which reveals the absurdity of leaving it undocumented and unpredictable. It also gently mocks the idea that any system would openly admit to providing undocumented failure modes.
sections.plainLanguage: The real joke is that computers did lose data and crash back then, and nobody documented it or controlled it. The RFC pretends to fix that by making it an official feature you can agree to, which is obviously silly.

sections.title: Implications
sections.content:
RFC 748 notes that servers which do not implement this option will be assumed to provide 100% reliable uptime. The joke is layered: not only is the option absurd, but the claim that any system not advertising RANDOMLY-LOSE is fully reliable is obviously false.

The RFC remained a joke. No TELNET implementation adopted the option, and no systems formally advertised random lossage. However, the document is valuable as a window into 1970s computer culture: it shows how frustrating and unreliable early networking systems were, and how the community responded with humor when faced with intractable problems.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not say you will randomly lose, people assume you will not. The joke is that was obviously not true in the 1970s; servers broke all the time without asking.
